threads_text: Elon Musk promised a full-length, historically accurate Odyssey movie made with Grok by the end of 2026. What arrived is a seven-minute Episode 1, and TechCrunch's reviewer called it airless. Would you watch a whole movie made by AI?
caption:
In July, Elon Musk said Grok Imagine would make a full-length, historically accurate Odyssey movie before the end of 2026.
On October 23, Grok posted the first seven minutes as Episode 1 of a series, made with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker.
TechCrunch's reviewer said some shots could pass for real actors at sea, but called the clip airless.

Would you watch a full movie made by AI?

site_article.answer_summary: Grok Imagine, xAI's video generator, released a seven-minute first episode of an AI-generated Odyssey series on X on October 23, 2026. It is not the full-length film Elon Musk promised in July, and a TechCrunch review called it airless.

paragraphs.text: Grok Imagine, the video generation tool from Elon Musk's xAI, posted seven minutes of an AI-generated adaptation of Homer's Odyssey on X on October 23, 2026. The post described the clip as Episode 1 of an Odyssey series, according to TechCrunch, which reviewed the footage on October 25.

The post credits Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker for what it called a creative collaboration. Startup Fortune reported that the episode runs 7 minutes and 12 seconds and was published in 4K resolution, and that xAI has not said which model version was used or how long the episode took to make.

According to LatestLY, the episode shows Odysseus preparing for the expedition to Troy, Penelope urging him to go, the Greek forces sailing for Troy and the training of his son Telemachus. The dialogue is in English, and TechCrunch noted that the narrator speaks with a British accent.
A smaller release than the July promise

In July 2026, Musk said Grok Imagine would make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that would be historically accurate, and that it would arrive before the end of the year. Startup Fortune pointed out that just over two months remain before that deadline, and that xAI is presenting the new clip as the opening chapter of a continuing series rather than a finished film.

Musk's pledge followed the July release of Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, which TechCrunch said relied mainly on practical filmmaking, with a shoot across six countries and a cast and crew of thousands. Startup Fortune reported that Nolan's film opened to a global debut of $264.1 million. Musk had criticized the casting of Nolan's film, according to TechCrunch and Cryptopolitan.
How the first episode was received

TechCrunch's Anthony Ha wrote that the footage was less ugly than he expected and better than Musk's recent AI videos, and that some shots could pass for real actors on a real sea. He said he could not judge its historical accuracy.

Ha was more critical of the storytelling. He described the clip as airless, said the voiceover backstory went on too long, called the dialogue stilted and wrote that there was little reason to care about the characters. He concluded that it was hard to imagine wanting another seven minutes, let alone a full movie. LatestLY also cited a Mashable review that pointed to familiar AI video flaws such as unnaturally perfect teeth and smudgy skin texture.

Startup Fortune reported that Grok Imagine's video tool can generate synchronized dialogue, sound effects and ambient audio, and that its clips are limited to 15 seconds each. The Grok post invited viewers to ask for a full breakdown of how the episode was made.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the episode shows how far AI video has come on individual shots and how much further it has to go on the parts of filmmaking that hold an audience, such as pacing, performance and character. A seven-minute episode built by a studio and a director also suggests that a long AI film still needs a lot of human work around the model.
The concrete test is whether xAI releases more episodes, or a full-length film, before December 31, 2026, the deadline Musk set in July.
